text: Young's modulus stands out as the most reliable predictor of build quality. Although it was not possible to directly quantify the amount of porosity present in the samples during this investigation, distinct trends are apparent, suggesting that the elastic moduli can be used to quickly identify patterns and correlations. These trends offer valuable insights into the relationships between processing conditions, material properties, and build quality, paving the way for further research into the development of predictive models for additive manufacturing. XCT High-resolution imaging of the samples was performed using the Zeiss X-ray Microscopy, Inc. Xradia 520 Versa system. The imaging parameters were carefully set to capture detailed information: 160kVp, 10W, 4x objective, 2401 projections, 9-second exposure, and a voxel size of 3.38 micrometers. Specifically, samples fabricated using the PAC powder in both as-built and heat-treated conditions were imaged. To gain a comprehensive understanding, the smallest and largest cylinders were imaged at the minimum and maximum parameters, respectively, as shown in Figures 20 and 21. The imaging results revealed that the diffusion layer, characterized by the interface of the bulk and contour parameters, is prone to void formation and accumulation throughout the sample. This phenomenon is attributed to the reduced lasing volume associated with smaller sizes, which can lead to increased porosity and defects in the additively manufactured parts. In stark contrast to the smaller cylinders, the 3mm cylinders exhibited a significant reduction in voids, which can be attributed to the increased lasing volume from the bulk parameter. The contour and diffusion layers in these larger cylinders are substantially smaller and confined to the outer perimeter, a desirable outcome. This configuration allows for the diffusion layer to be effectively factored into the design and subsequently removed through post-processing, thereby eliminating the voids. Furthermore, this optimal arrangement leaves room for future exploration of alternative diffusion layer options, enabling the development of more sophisticated and void- free additive manufacturing techniques. Notably, the heat treatment process, which involved exposing the samples to 650°C for 24 hours, failed to completely eliminate the voids. This suggests that a more aggressive approach may be necessary to achieve void-free samples. Future post-processing strategies could involve exploring higher heat treatment temperatures or considering alternative methods such as HIP to effectively mitigate the presence of voids and enhance the overall quality of the AM parts.
